items.title: Quantum Algorithms for Computational Fluid Dynamics
items.authors: Mario Guillaume Cecile, Nis-Luca van Hülst, Tomohiro Hashizume, Pia Siegl, Abhishek Setty, José Diogo da Costa Jesus, Paul Over, Sergio Bengoechea, Muhammad Umer, Spyros Tserkis, Eleftherios Mastorakis, Tristan Kraft, Francisco Cárdenas-López, Leonardo Scandurra, Thomas Rung, Felix Motzoi, Belda Yesil, Barbara Kraus, Martin Kiffner, Dimitris G. Angelakis, Eugene de Villiers, Dieter Jaksch
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Assesses fully quantum (QLSA, QSVT, QLBM) and hybrid (QPINN, amplitude-encoded VQA, TP-VQA) partial differential equation solvers for computational fluid dynamics. Finds asymptotic speedup is constrained by condition numbers, state preparation, operator compilation, and classical measurement bottlenecks.
items.question: Where can quantum computing algorithms offer genuine computational advantages over optimized classical solvers and tensor network methods in computational fluid dynamics?
items.limits: End-to-end advantage requires efficient state preparation and observable extraction without full classical state reconstruction; current evaluations limited mainly to 1D and simplified benchmark equations.
items.tools: quantum linear system algorithms · tensor-programmable variational quantum algorithms · quantum lattice Boltzmann methods · quantum physics-informed neural networks · matrix product states and operators
items.caption: Overview of the tensor-programmable variational quantum algorithm (TP-VQA) workflow, showing matrix product operator compilation of partial differential equation operators into quantum circuits alongside variational state optimization.
items.abstract: We present a comprehensive review of quantum approaches for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) arising in computational fluid dynamics (CFD). We examine fully quantum approaches, including quantum linear system algorithms (QLSAs), ranging from the Harrow--Hassidim--Lloyd (HHL) algorithm to quantum singular value transformation (QSVT), Hamiltonian simulation, and quantum lattice Boltzmann methods (QLBMs), while emphasizing hybrid quantum--classical approaches, including quantum physics-informed neural networks (QPINNs) and amplitude-encoded variational PDE solvers. We focus on hardware-agnostic algorithms compatible with present noisy processors and emerging fault-tolerant architectures. For each framework, we analyze the mathematical formulation, algorithmic structure, and principal limitations. We also examine tensor-network (TN) representations, since CFD fields, differential operators, and geometrical information can often be encoded efficiently in low-rank form. The TN formalism bridges CFD discretizations and quantum states, operators, and circuits, enabling compact representations to be translated into tensor-programmable variational quantum algorithms (TP-VQAs). We further review benchmark problems, including Poisson, reaction, diffusion, and nonlinear model equations, and assess how well quantum algorithms capture key features of fluid dynamics. Our analysis highlights that potential quantum advantage is highly problem dependent and governed by condition number, representational complexity, state preparation, and measurement constraints. We outline capabilities, limitations, and challenges toward scalable quantum algorithms for CFD.

items.title: A physical and universal model of bosonic computations with Solovay-Kitaev theorem
items.authors: Dorian Rudolph, Arsalan Motamedi, Dhruva Sambrani, Hamid Reza Naeij, Ulysse Chabaud, Sevag Gharibian, Saeed Mehraban
items.matched: Practical quantum advantage in quantum simulation
items.result: Bosonic Energy-Preserving Quantum Computation (BEQC) model uses energy-conserving gates driven by coherent state ancillae, efficiently simulating polynomial-energy continuous-variable circuits while recovering BQP and enabling Solovay-Kitaev gate compilation.
items.question: How can continuous-variable quantum computation be formulated to prevent unphysical energy blowups and restore universal compilation?
items.prior: Standard Lloyd-Braunstein continuous-variable models allow doubly exponential energy growth in time t, diverging photon numbers, and lack general Solovay-Kitaev compilation guarantees.
items.limits: Simulations of active non-energy-preserving operations require coherent ancilla amplitude α to scale with target precision O(1/ε); computational equivalence to BQP holds specifically in the polynomial-energy regime.
items.tools: Coherent state ancillae · Energy-preserving Hamiltonians · Linear optics and Kerr non-linearities · Lie-Trotter product formulas · Fock space truncation
items.caption: Schematic of the BEQC architecture: vacuum state inputs alongside a coherent-state energy reservoir undergo a sequence of energy-preserving unitaries before final photon-number measurement.
items.abstract: Bosonic quantum systems are among the leading architectures for quantum information processing, offering continuous-variable degrees of freedom with strong error-correction capabilities. However, standard bosonic quantum computation models such as the Lloyd-Braunstein [Lloyd and Braunstein, 1999] and hybrid oscillator-qubit models [Brenner, Dias, and Koenig, 2025; Liu et al., 2026] permit dramatic energy growth, leading to unphysical computational power and the breakdown of fundamental algorithmic tools such as universal and efficient compilation [Brenner et al., 2026; Rudolph et al., 2025]. To address this, we introduce a new model of bosonic quantum computation, Bosonic Energy-Preserving Quantum Computation (BEQC), in which energy is treated as a computational resource. Namely, energy is supplied solely through input coherent states, and all gates are generated by energy-preserving Hamiltonians. Thus, by construction, dramatic energy growth is impossible, making the model physically grounded. We next show that BEQC is a computationally robust and universal model in many respects, including: (1. Computational power) BEQC efficiently simulates all polynomial-energy computations in existing models, and exactly recovers BQP in the polynomial energy setting. It further admits several complexity-theoretic upper bounds when varying the energy, precision, and space parameters of the model. (2. Universal gate sets and state synthesis) BEQC has natural universal gate sets based on linear optics and Kerr interactions. In particular, we obtain a Solovay-Kitaev theorem which circumvents previous no-go results. We give various applications, including (a) a protocol for engineering GKP states with rigorous preparation guarantees, (b) Fock state preparation to exponential precision, and (c) native Fock space simulation of any qubit-based unitary.

items.title: All-Microwave Multiqubit Gates
items.authors: Guanqi Wang, Yao Song, Peng-Bo Li, Xiu-Hao Deng
items.matched: transmon and fluxonium coherence, single- and two-qubit gate fidelity
items.result: Single-step (n+m) multiqubit gates implemented on transmon networks via cross-resonance drives without tunable couplers. Three-qubit gates reach simulated fidelities >99.9% in 60ns.
items.question: How can single-step multiqubit gates with n control and m target transmons be implemented with all-microwave control without tunable couplers?
items.limits: Numerical simulation only. Dispersive regime with shared or near-degenerate target frequencies and suppressed parasitic terms such as ZXX.
items.tools: cross-resonance microwave drives · quad frame rotation · block diagonalization · gradient-based pulse optimization
items.caption: Gate infidelity versus optimization iteration and target Pauli operation fidelity across three-qubit gates and larger multi-target configurations, showing convergence below 10⁻³.
items.abstract: Implementing high-fidelity multiqubit gates is critical for reducing circuit depth in near-term quantum processors and fault-tolerant architectures. However, realizing multiqubit interactions and entanglement remains a critical challenge that limits the implementation of multiqubit gates. Here we propose an all-microwave scheme to realize single-step multiqubit gates incorporating n control and m target qubits, tailored for frequency-tunable superconducting transmon networks. By leveraging cross-resonance (CR) drives, this approach induces effective two-body ZX interactions that are significantly stronger than those achieved in conventional resonant regimes, circumventing the need for tunable couplers. The system's effective Hamiltonian is analytically derived using both quad frame rotation and rigorous block diagonalization. These combined theoretical methods facilitate the identification of optimal parameter regimes that simultaneously enhance desired target couplings and suppress parasitic higher-order terms, such as ZXX interactions. Through numerical simulations and gradient-based pulse-shape optimization, we demonstrate three-qubit gates achieving fidelities exceeding 99.9% within a 60 ns gate duration. Furthermore, we evaluate the fundamental scalability of this framework by extending the optimization to a five-qubit CXXXX architecture, confirming the physical viability of the multi-target driving scheme. Because these multiqubit operations naturally emulate stabilizer measurements, this architecture provides a hardware-efficient strategy for reducing the circuit depth of stabilizer-type operations by replacing sequential two-qubit gate decompositions with single-step multiqubit gates.

items.title: Reservoir- and Measurement-free Microwave Initialization of Semiconductor Spin Qubits
items.authors: Leon C. Camenzind, Ik Kyeong Jin, Akito Noiri, Kenta Takeda, Takashi Nakajima, Takashi Kobayashi, Seigo Tarucha
items.matched: Silicon quantum electronics
items.result: Fixed-sequence microwave and baseband initialization prepares singlet-associated charge state with 99.4% median probability without electron reservoirs or measurement feedback. Sequence uses ~12 μs of microwave bursts and mixing dwells in Si/SiGe quantum dots.
items.question: Can semiconductor spin-qubit pairs be initialized rapidly using only fixed microwave and baseband pulses, without local reservoir exchange or active measurement-based feedback?
items.limits: Single-cycle transfer bounded by 0.5 dark-state limit; total time excludes fixed baseband transport overheads and readout verification.
items.tools: three-qubit Si/SiGe device · electric-dipole spin resonance · radio-frequency reflectometry · Pauli spin blockade
items.caption: Measured initialization probability as a function of cycle repetitions for different initial spin states, showing convergence to >99% singlet state via repeated microwave-driven triplet transfer and mixing dwells.
items.abstract: Scalable quantum processors require repeated qubit initialization throughout large arrays. In semiconductor spin qubits, fast initialization commonly relies on local reservoir access or measurement-based feedback, requiring dedicated infrastructure that becomes increasingly difficult to distribute as processors scale. Here, we demonstrate reservoir- and measurement-free initialization of a silicon spin-qubit pair in an industrially fabricated Si/SiGe quantum-dot device using a fixed sequence of microwave and baseband pulses. Odd spin-parity states relax to the singlet charge state, whereas blocked even spin-parity states are microwave-driven through the triplet manifold and subsequently converted to the singlet by singlet-triplet mixing and charge hybridization. Repeated cycles produce the singlet-associated charge outcome with a median probability of 99.4% across the sampled preparation states, while exchange spectroscopy independently verifies mapping to the target |↑↓⟩ operational state. Microwave spectroscopy and time-domain measurements identify the dark-state-limited single-cycle transfer and the subsequent blockade-lifting dynamics that set the initialization time scale. The demonstrated pumping sequence uses approximately 12 μs of microwave bursts and mixing dwells, while we project sub-microsecond initialization under improved device conditions. These results establish fixed-sequence microwave initialization as a scalable control primitive for semiconductor spin-qubit processors, based on singlet-triplet physics that can be adapted to platforms with suitable Pauli-blockade transitions.

items.title: Qantum Well Resonant Tunneling Diode Probe of Correlated States in Twisted Bilayer MoS₂
items.authors: Chengjie Zhou, Jin-Xin Hu, Sihong Xu, Zijing Jin, Hui Li, Kam Tuen Law, Jiannong Wang
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Near-AB-stacked ≈57^∘ tMoS₂ exhibits a robust correlated insulating state at ν=1 across all measured displacement fields, and an emergent fractional insulating state at ν=3/4 for D < -75mV/nm that disappears above 12K.
items.question: Can correlated electronic states in the electron-doped flat bands of near-AB-stacked twisted bilayer MoS₂ be probed locally with dual-gate field control?
items.limits: Tested on two devices (twist angles ≈57^∘ and ≈56.5^∘) at temperatures from 1.7K to 100K and magnetic fields up to 9T.
items.tools: quantum well resonant tunneling diode (QWRTD) · vertical tunneling differential conductance (dI/dV_Probe) · dual-gate electrostatics · twisted bilayer MoS₂
items.caption: Differential conductance dI/dV_Probe versus filling factor ν and vertical displacement field D at 2K. Dips mark the continuous insulating state at ν=1 and the emergent fractional state at ν=3/4 below -75mV/nm.
items.abstract: Moiré superlattices formed in transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) offer a versatile platform for exploring emergent quantum phases arising from strong electronic correlations. In this work, we develop a new experimental platform, the quantum well resonant tunneling diode (QWRTD), to probe the electronic landscape of ≈57^∘ twisted bilayer MoS₂ (tMoS₂). By measuring the differential conductance (dI/dV_Probe) as a function of filling factor ν and displacement field D, we observe a robust integer correlated insulating state at ν= 1 that persists across the measured displacement field range. Furthermore, we identify a displacement-field-induced fractional insulating state at ν= 3/4 for D < -75~mV/nm. Temperature- and magnetic-field-dependent measurements characterize this ν= 3/4 state as a potential generalized Wigner crystal. These correlated states are also observed in another device with a similar twist angle (≈56.5^∘). Our results provide direct evidence of correlated states in near-AB-stacked tMoS₂ and establish QWRTD as a powerful experimental tool for investigating strong correlations and topology in van der Waals heterostructures.

items.title: Quantum double lock-in detection via sequential orthogonal quantum mixing
items.authors: Min Zhuang, Sijie Chen, Jiahao Huang, Chaohong Lee
items.matched: circuit QED dispersive readout and Purcell-limited measurement
items.result: Single-interferometer quantum double lock-in detection extracts amplitude A, frequency ω, and initial phase β of an oscillating signal, achieving Heisenberg-limited precisions ΔA, Δω, Δβ∝1/N with an N-particle GHZ probe and interaction-based readout.
items.question: Can quantum double lock-in detection extract full amplitude, frequency, and phase information from an unknown oscillating signal using a single quantum interferometry while achieving Heisenberg-limited precision?
items.prior: Conventional quantum double lock-in detection requires two separate quantum interferometers, each requiring state preparation and readout (was ∝1/√N scaling without entanglement).
items.limits: Theoretical derivation assuming instantaneous π pulses and noiseless state initialization. Gaussian detection noise σ= 0.5√N degrades scaling to between SQL and Heisenberg limit.
items.tools: Periodic dynamical decoupling (PDD) sequences · Carr-Purcell (CP) sequences · Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states · Fast Fourier transform (FFT) / Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) analysis
items.caption: Log-log scaling of measurement precisions ΔA, Δω, and Δβ versus particle number N, showing 1/√N standard quantum limit for spin-coherent states and 1/N Heisenberg scaling for GHZ states.
items.abstract: High-precision measurement of oscillating signal is a ubiquitous issue in fundamental science and a critical task in practical technologies. In quantum metrology, quantum lock-in detection provide an efficient method for measuring such signal. In general, when the initial phase of the oscillating signal is unknown,quantum double lock-in detection can effectively extract complete information about the signal's amplitude, frequency, and initial phase. Conventional quantum double lock-in detection requires two individual quantum interferometry, each of which must undergo state preparation and readout. However, the time for state preparation and readout need not be negligible in practical experiments. In particular, the time for state preparation is longer than the time for sensing. To save experimental resources, it is challenging to achieve quantum double lock-in detection just via a single quantum interferometry while still extracting complete information about the signal's amplitude, frequency, and initial phase. Here, we present a general protocol for achieving a quantum double lock-in detection just via a single quantum interferometry under a sequential orthogonal periodic multipulse sequences. In particular, if the input state is a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state and two interaction-based operations are applied during interferometry, the measurement precisions for frequency, amplitude, and initial phase can both approach the Heisenberg limit. Our study paves a new way for measuring oscillating signals with a single quantum interferometry, and provides a feasible method for achieving Heisenberg-limited detection of alternating signals.

items.title: Multi-Branch Transport in a Back-gated WS₂ Transistor at Deep-Cryogenic Temperature
items.authors: Megan Powell, Vilas Patil, Hazel Neill, Stephen O'Sullivan, Paul K. Hurley, Lida Ansari, Farzan Gity, Alessandro Rossi
items.matched: materials-limited loss: two-level systems, interfaces, valley splitting
items.result: Back-gated multilayer WS₂ transistor operates down to 20~mK with an on/off current ratio >10⁵ and reproducible multi-stage turn-on shoulders described by parallel conduction branches.
items.question: How do the electrical transport and turn-on characteristics of a back-gated multilayer WS₂ field-effect transistor evolve at deep-cryogenic temperatures down to the millikelvin regime?
items.prior: was on/off ratio ≈10⁴ at 77~K for WSe₂ devices (reference 16)
items.limits: Single back-gated device on Si/SiO₂ with Ni/Au contacts; transport influenced by contact barriers, trap states, and electrostatic disorder.
items.tools: mechanically exfoliated multilayer WS₂ flake (∼90~nm) · dilution refrigerator (20~mK ≤T ≤25~K) · multi-branch Lambert-W conduction model · density functional theory (DFT)
items.caption: Drain current I_DS plotted against back-gate voltage V_GS from 20~mK to 25~K at V_DS = 0.5~V, showing multi-stage turn-on and extracted on/off current ratios exceeding 10⁵ across the full temperature range.
items.abstract: Two-dimensional materials are promising candidates for electronic applications beyond the operating limits of conventional semiconductor technologies. Within this class, transition-metal dichalcogenides offer attractive properties for field-effect transistor operation, with tungsten disulphide (WS₂) emerging as a particularly promising material for operation at cryogenic temperatures. Here, we investigate the electrical performance of a back-gated multilayer WS₂ transistor at deep cryogenic temperature, down to 20 mK. The device remains strongly gate-tunable throughout the cryogenic regime, with an effective on/off current ratio exceeding 10⁵. Most notably, the low-temperature turn-on characteristics exhibit reproducible shoulder-like features, which we describe using a phenomenological model comprising multiple effective conduction branches operating in parallel.

items.title: Optical observation of interlayer spin correlation
items.authors: Akiyoshi Park, Pranshoo Upadhyay, Andrey Grankin, Emil Viñas Boström, Mahdi Ghafariasl, Hassan Alnatah, Masoud Mohammadi-Arzanagh, Gautam Nambiar, Beini Gao, Alireza Alvandi, Sakthi Rajmano Madhan Kumar, Ghadah Alshalan, Isaac Sherwood, Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad, You Zhou, Arun Ramanathan, Xavier Roy, Angel Rubio, Mohammad Hafezi

items.result: Two-magnon Raman scattering measures dynamical interlayer spin correlations ⟨(hatS_A·hatS_B)(t)(hatS_A·hatS_B)(0)⟩, observing two-magnon features at 46 meV and 82 meV in CrSBr that vanish above T_C∼150K and collapse under out-of-plane field as (1 - (B/B_sat)²)². Exciton-resonant excitation at 908 nm enhances two-magnon intensity roughly tenfold.
items.question: Can interlayer spin–spin correlations in layered van der Waals antiferromagnets be directly probed by optical spectroscopy?
items.limits: Measured on bulk CrSBr at T=3.5K; two-magnon channel vanishes in field-induced ferromagnetic state above B_sat≈2.1T.
items.tools: Two-magnon Raman spectroscopy · Fleury–Loudon light–matter interaction modeling · CrSBr van der Waals antiferromagnet · Exciton resonance enhancement
items.caption: Measured (top) and calculated (bottom) Raman spectrum of CrSBr versus Raman shift. Shows three sharp low-frequency A_g phonon peaks and a broad two-magnon continuum spanning ∼45to100meV with band edge at 46meV and peak at 82meV.
items.abstract: Spin correlations govern numerous collective behaviors of quantum materials, underpinning exotic phenomena such as unconventional superconductivity and topological magnetism. In layered materials, the interlayer spin correlation is important because it characterizes the magnetic ground state and determines spin transport across the interface. Yet interlayer spin correlations have remained hard to measure directly, leaving one of the most basic quantities of two-dimensional magnetism out of experimental reach. Here we provide the first direct optical probe of interlayer spin correlations, using two-magnon Raman scattering in the van der Waals antiferromagnet (AFM) CrSBr, in remarkable agreement with a microscopic spin-wave model without any fitting parameter. Moreover, the two-magnon channel switches on only in the AFM state and vanishes when a magnetic field takes the crystal to a ferromagnetic state. We furthermore establish an exciton-mediated variant of the technique, where tuning the laser near the exciton resonance enhances the signal roughly tenfold due to the exciton's large oscillator strength. Magnon-pair Raman spectroscopy thus opens a direct optical window into interlayer spin correlations in van der Waals magnets, extendable to twisted bilayers and proximity-coupled heterostructures.

items.title: Complex Quantum Dynamics Versus Classical Simulability of Noisy Random Circuits
items.authors: Anjali Waghmare, Sergii Strelchuk, Sathyawageeswar Subramanian
items.matched: Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play
items.result: Dynamical diagnostics (magic, scrambling, anticoncentration, non-Gaussianity) decouple from classical simulation hardness in noisy quantum circuits. Local depolarising noise damps fourth-order Pauli moments asymptotically twice as fast as second-order moments, causing magic to vanish at depth Θ(N) while efficient classical sampling threshold remains Θ(1) under sparse noise.
items.question: In noisy quantum circuits, do dynamical diagnostics such as magic, scrambling, and anticoncentration reliably track classical simulability?
items.limits: Depolarising noise on brickwork Clifford+T and Majorana dephasing on matchgate+SWAP circuits.
items.tools: fourth-order Clifford commutant · Pauli-path truncation · Majorana transfer matrix · replica transfer matrix
items.caption: Circuit depth versus depolarising noise parameter (or dephasing parameter). Dashed curves mark dynamical resource boundaries; solid colors mark fastest classical simulation algorithms, showing the dynamical boundary crosscuts classical simulation efficiency regions in both directions.
items.abstract: Claims of quantum advantage rest on the classical hardness of simulating quantum circuits. Magic, operator scrambling, anticoncentration, and non-Gaussianity for fermionic circuits are standard diagnostics of complex quantum dynamics. For pure states, some of these have been rigorously connected to classical simulability. Whether these diagnostics reliably track the limits of efficient classical simulation under noise remains unclear. Here, we show that in noisy Clifford+T and nearest-neighbour matchgate+SWAP circuits, dynamical diagnostics and classical simulability can separate in both directions. In particular, the diagnostics can remain nontrivial after classical simulation becomes efficient, or become trivial before known efficient classical algorithms apply. We trace this mismatch to the different statistical properties they probe: magic and scrambling depend on fourth-order statistics of the Pauli spectrum, whereas the simulation algorithms depend primarily on second-order moments, which local noise suppresses at different rates. Thus, dynamical diagnostics measured on a noisy quantum device do not by themselves constitute evidence for classical hardness.

items.title: CSS codes for Quantum Metrology with Discrete-time Error Correction
items.authors: Ugnė Liaubaitė, Debora Ramacciotti, Robert Raußendorf
items.matched: Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play
items.result: Discrete-time CSS quantum error correction preserves Heisenberg-like temporal scaling δω∝T⁻¹ against perpendicular noise within an interrogation window scaling as t_p ∼1/τ, before crossing over to SQL-like scaling δω∝T^(-1/2). Single recovery applied solely at interrogation end yields zero metrological advantage.
items.question: How does finite-frequency discrete error correction with Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes preserve parameter sensitivity and affect the Heisenberg-to-SQL crossover under perpendicular Markovian noise?
items.limits: Instantaneous and ideal recovery operations; initial logical-plus state |+_L⟩^(⊗k) without noise optimization; local Z signal Hamiltonian and perpendicular Markovian X noise.
items.tools: CSS stabilizer codes (Steane, Shor) · Adjoint Lindblad master equation · Discrete syndrome extraction and recovery map · Classical Fisher information of stabilizer projector
items.caption: Frequency sensitivity versus total sensing time budget T for Steane and Shor codes across correction intervals τ. Sensitivity scales linearly (T⁻¹) up to optimal interrogation time t_opt, then transitions to square-root scaling (T^(-1/2)).
items.abstract: The goal of quantum metrology is to estimate an unknown parameter with better-than-classical precision and, ideally, to attain Heisenberg scaling. In realistic settings, however, noise can substantially reduce this advantage and, in many cases, restore standard-quantum-limit-like performance. Preserving the quantum enhancement therefore requires noise-robust strategies, which can be implemented using quantum error correction. In this work, we develop and analyze a quantum-metrology protocol based on Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes. The main result is that, for noise perpendicular to the sensing Hamiltonian, discrete-time error correction preserves Heisenberg-like temporal scaling over a finite interrogation-time window whose duration depends on the correction frequency. It is further shown that recovery applied only after the sensing evolution provides no metrological advantage over the corresponding uncorrected noisy protocol in the setup considered here. An analytical framework is developed for arbitrary CSS codes and applied to the Steane and Shor codes, for which the discrete-time corrected dynamics, the Heisenberg-like-to-SQL-like crossover, and the optimal interrogation time are determined and numerically analysed.

items.title: Quantum synchronization in atom-cavity coupled systems
items.authors: Katha Haldar, Anushree Dey, Saikat Ghosh, Bimalendu Deb
items.matched: cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks
items.result: Atom-mediated coupling induces limit cycles in undriven cavity modes and out-of-phase quantum synchronization when driven weakly, with Wehrl mutual information showing strict anti-correlation with field synchronization.
items.question: Can atom-mediated coupling between two driven cavity modes induce a two-mode quantum limit cycle and generate phase-locked field dynamics?
items.limits: Requires strong-coupling cavity QED regime with cavity decay rates κ₁, κ₂ ≪g₁, g₂, Ω_i, and large excited-state detuning |Δ_d| ≫g_i, Ω, Γ_d.
items.tools: effective operator adiabatic elimination · SU(2) coherent states over Fock subspaces · generalized two-mode Husimi-Q function · Wehrl mutual information · quantum trajectory method
items.caption: Husimi-Q distribution Q_field(θ,φ), synchronization measure S_field(φ), and single-mode Wigner distributions W_i(x_i,p_i) for weak cavity drives Ω₁=Ω₂=0.005Γ_d, showing phase localization and out-of-phase synchronization across the two cavity modes.
items.abstract: We consider a cavity quantum electrodynamics (CQED) setup where an ensemble of spin-1 atoms driven by a classical field interacts with two driven cavity field modes. We show that the two sub-systems - the atoms and the two-mode cavity field, exhibit limit-cycle or quantum synchronization depending on the cavity drive strengths and other system parameters. In order to visualize the limit cycle and synchronization in the field, we introduce generalized two-mode field Husimi-Q function using SU(2) coherent states. For atomic spin states, we make use of spin-1 Husimi-Q function to visualize the same. We further corroborate the occurrence of field synchronization and limit cycle by analyzing U(1) symmetry breaking, Wigner quasi-probability distribution, coherence properties of reduced field density matrix. Our results reveal intriguing interplay between the limit-cycle and quantum synchronization behavior, highlighting emergent quantum phenomena in driven dissipative interacting quantum systems. Additionally, we calculate Wehrl mutual information between the two modes and find that the field synchronization and Wehrl mutual information are mutually exclusive. Our study would be important to extract quantum advantages in quantum metrology using coupled atom-cavity systems.

items.title: Loss-tolerant distributed lattice surgery using fusion networks
items.authors: Felix Burt, Richard Meister, Sheng-Ku Lin, Kuan-Cheng Chen, Michael Hanks, Roberto Bondesan, M. S. Kim, Kin K. Leung
items.matched: Cavity-based quantum networks with single atoms and optical photons
items.result: Hybrid fusion-network protocols for distributed rotated surface code lattice surgery achieve a 50% interface-erasure threshold without local noise. Increases merge-observable interface distance from d+1 to 2d+1 and restores perpendicular-observable distance from lfloor(d+1)/2rfloor to d.
items.question: How can photonic fusion networks and resource states be integrated to make distributed lattice surgery between QPUs robust against photon loss and erasure?
items.prior: Straight Bell-pair interface geometry had merge interface distance d+1 and perpendicular interface distance lfloor(d+1)/2rfloor.
items.limits: Numerical and theoretical analysis assuming phenomenological erasure, circuit-level Pauli noise, and resource-state noise models; interface-distance advantage masked when local noise reaches 10⁻³, becoming effective at 10⁻⁴ and below.
items.tools: ZX-calculus transformations · fusion-based quantum computing · rotated surface codes · distributed lattice surgery · linear cluster states
items.abstract: Networking matter-based quantum processing units (QPUs) offers a promising route to scaling fault-tolerant quantum computers. This requires distributed logical operations to be performed across photonic links, where noise is characteristically different from and stronger than in local QPUs owing to photon loss and probabilistic linear-optical operations. Measurement- and fusion-based quantum computing are designed to be robust against loss and probabilistic photonic operations, suggesting they could complement circuit-based error correction at the interface between networked QPUs. We use ZX calculus transformations to construct hybrid syndrome extraction protocols and apply them to distributed rotated surface code lattice surgery, demonstrating that several protocols attain a 50% interface-erasure threshold when local noise is absent, including circuit-based lattice surgery using fused Bell pairs and hybrid protocols using linear cluster states. Relative to a straight Bell-pair interface geometry, the hybrid protocols increase the merge-observable interface distance from d+1 to 2d+1 and restore the perpendicular-observable interface distance from lfloor(d+1)/2rfloor to d. We calculate how the threshold decreases when using truncated resource states and map correctable regions under resource-state errors, local circuit noise, and fusion erasure. We then convert these erasure thresholds into photon-loss thresholds and probe subthreshold performance using fusion boosting. At circuit and resource-state error rates of 10⁻³, local errors largely mask the interface-distance advantage. As local noise is reduced to 10⁻⁴ and below, the linear-chain protocols improve more rapidly with decreasing erasure, suggesting that interface distance enhancements are effective in low local noise regimes.

items.title: esQueranto: Differentiable Structured Quantum Light for Automated Scientific Discovery
items.authors: Marcello Armezzani, Tareq Jaouni, Pontus Lindgren, Sören Arlt, Mario Krenn, Xuemei Gu
items.matched: cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks
items.result: Unified differentiable simulation combines Fock-state quantum optics with structured-light propagation in JAX, allowing mode-dependent Gouy phases and lenses to directly alter Fock bases and quantum interference.
items.question: How can photon-number quantum optics, open-system noise, and transverse spatial-mode propagation be unified into a single differentiable simulator for automated experimental design?
items.prior: Existing tools separately model photonic quantum optics (MrMustard, Perceval) or wave optics (XLuminA, Chromatix) without combining Fock states and spatial propagation in a differentiable framework.
items.limits: Classical pump approximation for squeezing; paraxial and Laguerre-Gauss beam assumptions without full non-paraxial vectorial propagation or open-system matter couplings.
items.tools: JAX automatic differentiation · Fock basis expansion · Laguerre-Gauss spatial mode propagation · interferometric radial-mode sorters
items.caption: Heralded radial-mode sorting output probabilities versus dephasing strength γ= 1 - ξ. Single-photon input routing degrades to equal split (1/2), while two-photon inputs (p=0, p=1) approach 3/4 anti-bunching due to common-path phase noise.
items.abstract: Uncovering new phenomena in nature requires experiments. For centuries, their design has been exclusively a human endeavor. Today, a new paradigm is emerging in which artificial intelligence and computational methods can design experiments themselves. Realizing this form of automated scientific discovery requires simulators that are sufficiently expressive to represent the diverse physical processes and couplings from which new experiments can be constructed. In this direction, we introduce textscesQueranto, a differentiable software that brings photon-number quantum optics and structured-light propagation into a common description, allowing the spatial evolution of light to directly influence non-classical quantum states and their interference. textscesQueranto is implemented in JAX, providing automatic differentiation and hardware-accelerated evaluation for optimization and automated search. We demonstrate the framework across a broad range of quantum-optical applications that exercise complementary aspects of its physical description. By combining quantum and structured-light physics within a single differentiable simulator, textscesQueranto takes an important step towards the dream of a foundational simulator in physics.

Single-photon input routing degrades to equal split (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>), while two-photon inputs (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>) approach <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> anti-bunching due to common-path phase noise.

items.title: First-quantized quantum simulation with non-local potentials by matrix-product-state encoding
items.authors: Kazuki Tsuoka, Taichi Kosugi, Masari Watanabe, Hirofumi Nishi, Yu-ichiro Matsushita
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Matrix product state encoding of non-local pseudopotentials yields a single Trotter step circuit depth of O(°(V_loc) n^(°(V_loc)) + 8Lnn_atomχ² + 2n²). For n = 7 qubits, depth is 1,747 versus 23,775 for direct unitary decomposition.
items.question: How to efficiently implement arbitrary non-local pseudopotentials within first-quantized quantum chemistry dynamics circuits?
items.prior: Direct dense unitary decomposition scaled exponentially as O(4ⁿ), reaching circuit depth 23,775 at n = 7.
items.limits: Demonstrated for a one-dimensional single-electron hydrogen ionization model in momentum representation. Assumes polynomial local potential V_loc and low bond dimension saturation for smooth projectors.
items.tools: matrix product state encoding · first-order Trotterization · binary-encoded wave functions · Qiskit transpiler unitary synthesis
items.caption: Circuit depth of a single Trotter step plotted against qubit count n for MPS bond dimensions χ= 2, 4, 6, 8 compared to standard unitary decomposition.
items.abstract: Quantum simulations based on first-quantized approaches can offer lower space and gate complexities than second-quantized approaches. The gate requirements for these simulations can be further reduced by employing pseudopotentials, a technique widely used in classical quantum chemistry calculations to decrease the number of simulated electrons. However, implementing pseudopotentials in quantum circuits remains challenging due to their non-local nature. In this study, we proposed a method to efficiently implement non-local potentials using matrix product state (MPS) encoding. MPS encoding allows us to efficiently implement a Trotter step operator with a circuit depth of O(deg(V_loc) n^(deg(V_loc)) + 8Lnn_atomχ² + 2n²), where deg(V_loc) is the degree of the polynomial local potential, n_atom is the number of atoms in the system, L is the maximum number of projector functions across all atoms, and n is the number of qubits used to represent the binary-encoded wave function in one-dimensional space. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a model of the ionization of a one-dimensional hydrogen atom driven by an ultrashort laser pulse. Our results showed that MPS encoding significantly reduces the required circuit depth compared to a direct unitary decomposition, providing a pathway for practical first-quantized simulations.

items.title: Quantum Circuit Pruning: From NISQ Architectures to Fault-Tolerant Operations
items.authors: Pau Escofet, Carmen G. Almudéver, Sergi Abadal, Eduard Alarcón
items.matched: Demonstration of a small programmable quantum computer with atomic qubits
items.result: Compares omission fidelity bound cos²(θ/2) against hardware routing costs, cutting two-qubit gate count by up to 48.6% and increasing circuit fidelity by up to 47.7% on NISQ benchmarks.
items.question: Can quantum circuit gate pruning be dynamically guided by routing distance and execution noise in both NISQ and fault-tolerant regimes?
items.prior: was offline gate pruning considering only rotation angle θ without target hardware connectivity constraints
items.limits: Evaluated via simulations on 4–14 qubit NISQ circuits and proxy two-CNOT lattice surgery paths rather than full end-to-end FTQC compilation; assumes fixed 1.25× SWAP routing overhead multiplier for NISQ heuristics.
items.tools: Route-Forcing algorithm · Stim and PyMatching simulation · TQEC lattice surgery · Qiskit density-matrix simulation
items.caption: Two-qubit CX gate counts (top) and final circuit state fidelities (bottom) plotted across 4- to 14-qubit benchmark algorithms for unpruned compilation versus the proposed routing-aware pruning.
items.abstract: We present a routing-aware pruning strategy for quantum circuits that selectively removes parametric two-qubit gates whose computational contribution is outweighed by the fidelity cost of their execution, and assess it across both Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) and fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) architectures. Each two-qubit gate of a circuit is evaluated by comparing an architecture-independent lower bound on the fidelity cost of omitting the gate against a hardware-specific model for the routing execution cost in each setting. We additionally provide an analytical characterization of the pruning boundary as a function of rotation angle, qubit distance, and hardware noise. Simulations on benchmark circuits demonstrate gate count reductions of up to 48.6% and fidelity improvements of up to 47.7% in the NISQ regime, while a feasibility analysis on FT hardware indicates that pruning is expected to remain relevant across a range of code distances and physical error rates. These results establish routing-aware pruning as a practical and unified compilation strategy across the quantum computing stack.

items.title: Nonlinear collective-spin dynamics for quantum-enhanced sensing in solid-state platforms
items.authors: Le Bin Ho
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Connects nonlinear collective-spin twisting dynamics to solid-state platforms, surveying spin squeezing and quantum enhancements across NV ensembles (demonstrating -0.50±0.13 dB squeezing or 6.7(6)% amplification), donor spins in ²⁸Si, and magnetic Kittel modes.
items.question: How do microscopic interactions, disorder, and decoherence dictate the generation of quantum-enhanced metrological states via nonlinear collective-spin dynamics in solid-state platforms?
items.limits: Spatial disorder and inhomogeneous couplings break collective permutation symmetry; technical noise, control errors, and decoherence cap effective nonlinear interaction time.
items.tools: Dicke basis collective spin formalism · one-axis and two-axis twisting (OAT/TAT) · Floquet pulse engineering · nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center ensembles · tqix simulation package
items.caption: Wineland squeezing parameter ξ² plotted against scaled evolution time χt, comparing noise reduction capabilities of one-axis twisting, two-axis twisting, and two-axis non-twisting dynamics.
items.abstract: Collective spin systems in solid-state materials are promising platforms for quantum-enhanced sensing. In systems such as nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, donor spins in silicon, and magnetic materials, interactions among many spins can generate collective quantum correlations that improve measurement precision beyond the standard quantum limit. This tutorial develops an intuitive, materials-oriented framework for understanding these effects through nonlinear collective-spin dynamics. We show how nonlinear interactions reshape collective spin states in phase space, redistribute quantum fluctuations, and generate metrologically useful states such as spin-squeezed and entangled states. We then connect these ideal collective dynamics to microscopic interactions and realistic solid-state systems, discussing how interaction strength, disorder, decoherence, and experimental control affect sensing performance. Different platforms and experiments are compared to highlight key material properties, advantages, and limitations. The tutorial focuses on a materials-oriented understanding of nonlinear collective-spin sensing, rather than a comprehensive comparison of experimental platforms or a practical guide to sensing experiments.

items.question: Can basis-independent quantum coherence for an ensemble of quantum states be quantified directly in experiment?

items.tools: Sagnac interferometer · spontaneous parametric down-conversion · PPKTP crystal · single-photon detectors

items.abstract: We present a direct experimental verification of quantum coherence for a set of quantum states in a basis-independent manner. We find that the theory of quantum coherence for a set of quantum states matches our experimental results perfectly and can be applied to protocols like BB84 and quantum secure direct communication. Using a Sagnac interferometer, we experimentally quantify the quantum coherence for two sets of experimental states. Moreover, we introduce a novel application of set coherence, illustrating that the states employed in the BB84 protocol exhibit maximal set coherence. Our results pave the way for wider applications of quantum coherence for a set of quantum states, including quantum key distribution protocols and probabilistic quantum cloning.

items.title: Less precise but less noisy: local circuits for momentum-space state preparation and measurement
items.authors: Etienne Granet, Henrik Dreyer
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Adiabatic state preparation reaches lower energies than Fermionic Fourier Transform (FFT) on noisy hardware for tight-binding chains with Ngtrapprox20 qubits at equal two-qubit gate counts. Noise heating per two-qubit gate scales as O(1) for FFT but remains constant O(1/N) for adiabatic evolution.
items.question: How does circuit noise sensitivity compare between high-precision Fermionic Fourier Transforms and local Hamiltonian simulation or adiabatic evolution for state preparation and measurement?
items.prior: FFT state preparation and momentum measurement (Ref [31]) exhibited high noise sensitivity due to global error propagation.
items.limits: Antiperiodic boundary conditions, tight-binding free-fermion chains, non-post-selected initial state |+...+⟩ introducing tiny energy shifts scaling as 1/N, fixed number of measurement shots (300 to 375).
items.tools: Quantinuum System Model H2-2 trapped-ion processor · Adiabatic evolution Trotter circuits · Momentum Distribution from Local Measurements (MDLM) · Jordan-Wigner transformation
items.caption: Measured energy density and energy increase per two-qubit gate versus system size N for FFT and adiabatic evolution on Quantinuum H2-2. Shows adiabatic evolution achieving lower energies than FFT above N≈20 due to constant heating per gate compared to linear growth for FFT.
items.abstract: Quantum algorithms are usually optimized for gate count or circuit depth. We find on Quantinuum System Model H2 quantum computer that for a tight-binding chain ground state preparation, there is a system size N beyond which the adiabatic evolution reaches significantly lower energies than the Fermionic Fourier Transform (FFT), with the same number of gates, and with the same circuit depth. We attribute this high noise sensitivity of the FFT to its high precision, being able to distinguish momenta by 1/N. This high resolution in momentum space requires long-range couplings in real space, which propagates errors faster. In contrast, although local and physical circuits such as the adiabatic evolution have a coarser momentum resolution, they also propagate errors more slowly. For physical applications, high momentum resolution is rarely required and is often worth trading for low noise sensitivity. We also introduce a momentum measurement scheme that although less precise than FFT, is less costly and less noisy. We show that it achieves better performance than FFT for spectral function measurement on Quantinuum System Model H2 quantum computer. Our work emphasizes the importance of reducing the noise sensitivity of quantum algorithms, beyond the number of gates or circuit depth.

items.question: Can a code-agnostic neural decoder achieve high decoding accuracy across diverse stabilizer codes and noise models using only the detection error model as input?
items.prior: was correlated MWPM for surface codes and BP+OSD for qLDPC codes
items.limits: Numerical simulations; accuracy drops when generalizing to unseen codes with graphs larger than the largest training graph.
items.tools: POLYMECHANON graph neural network · Stim detection error model tripartite graph · residual message passing with GRU · confidence-based post-selection
items.caption: Logical error rate versus physical error rate p for rotated surface codes (d=3 to 9) and qLDPC LaCross codes under phenomenological and circuit-level noise, comparing the GNN decoder to correlated MWPM and BP+OSD baselines.
items.abstract: We present POLYMECHANON, a graph neural network (GNN) decoder for quantum error correction whose only input is the detection error model (DEM) of a quantum code under a given noise model. We represent the DEM as a tripartite graph of detectors, error mechanisms and logical observables, where every input feature is computed by using the quantum code as data rather than design choice. In this way, the same architecture decodes in principle any stabiliser code, under any noise model that can be expressed as a detection error model, once trained on the DEM. We test this approach along four directions. Firstly, on the rotated surface code the decoder outperforms correlated MWPM under both phenomenological and circuit-level noise, with up to 25% fewer logical failures. Secondly, on a family of high-rate qLDPC codes it matches BP+OSD on the smaller codes and surpasses it on the larger ones, with up to 16% fewer logical failures on [ [130,4,6] ]. Thirdly, its decoding time does not depend on the physical error rate, whereas that of BP+OSD grows with it: on [ [130,4,6] ] its effective cost per shot is of the order of a few ms on a single GPU against a few tens of milliseconds for BP+OSD on a single CPU core, and its fixed computational graph makes it a candidate for real-time decoding on neutral-atom processors. Finally, a single model trained across codes of different families outperforms uncorrelated MWPM on the graph-like codes seen during training and stays within 10% of BP+OSD on the others, while it tends to fail to generalize to unseen codes, particularly larger ones. Its probabilistic output enables confidence-based post-selection, lowering the logical error rate by more than an order of magnitude on the surface code while keeping more than 90% of the shots. Since only the DEM changes, new codes and noise models can be decoded without redesigning the decoder.

items.title: Trapdoored Clifford Operators and Applications
items.authors: Minki Hhan, Hojune Lee
items.matched: How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits
items.result: Constructed trapdoored n-qubit Clifford operators sampled and implemented with n^(1+ε) elementary gates (or n·polylog(n) under subexponential hardness) in polylogarithmic depth, computationally indistinguishable from uniform random Cliffords.
items.question: Can the quadratic gate complexity and linear depth of sampling and implementing uniform random n-qubit Clifford operators be bypassed using pseudorandom trapdoored distributions?
items.prior: Sampling and implementing uniformly random n-qubit Cliffords took O(n²) time with size Θ(n²/logn) circuits (Bravyi and Maslov 2021).
items.limits: Relies on the computational hardness of the (dual) ring-LPN assumption; circuits require all-to-all connectivity for polylogarithmic depth and use n^(1+ε) clean ancillary qubits.
items.tools: (dual) ring learning parity with noise (LPN) assumption · trapdoored matrix distributions · Bruhat decomposition · Bravyi–Maslov Clifford sampler
items.abstract: Random Clifford operators have numerous applications in quantum computing, including randomized benchmarking, classical shadows, and quantum authentication. However, sampling and implementing uniformly random n-qubit Clifford incur near-quadratic complexity due to the size of Clifford group. We introduce a cryptographic way to overcome these barriers: trapdoored Clifford operator distributions whose samples are computationally indistinguishable from uniformly random Cliffords, yet implementing them can be much faster given the trapdoor. We construct a distribution of trapdoored Clifford operators whose elements can be sampled and implemented in near-linear time under a variant of the learning parity with noise assumption. Our constructions allow fast tableau action on Pauli labels for classical simulation, and also can be optimized to admit polylogarithmic-depth implementation. Along the way, we construct trapdoored matrices over finite fields that support efficient multiplication by both a matrix and its inverse, resolving an open question left by Vaikuntanathan and Zamir [SODA'26]. We use these constructions to obtain faster protocols based on random Cliffords. We also explore their applications to the worst-case to average-case reductions for matrix and Clifford problems including the iterated matrix multiplication and Clifford circuit synthesis. In particular, we show the hardness of batching Clifford circuits: synthesizing circuits that apply the same Clifford to multiple registers is at least as hard as worst-case matrix multiplication, even when synthesis succeeds on a small constant fraction of random Cliffords. This extends to approximate implementations by general quantum circuits.

items.title: Loss-tolerant distributed lattice surgery using fusion networks
items.authors: Felix Burt, Richard Meister, Sheng-Ku Lin, Kuan-Cheng Chen, Michael Hanks, Roberto Bondesan, M. S. Kim, Kin K. Leung
items.matched: Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery
items.result: Hybrid fusion-network protocols for distributed rotated surface code lattice surgery reach a 50% interface-erasure threshold without local noise. They increase merge-observable interface distance from d+1 to 2d+1 and restore perpendicular-observable interface distance from lfloor(d+1)/2rfloor to d.
items.question: How to design loss-tolerant distributed lattice surgery protocols across photonic links between networked quantum processing units using fusion networks?
items.prior: Straight Bell-pair interface geometry had merge-observable interface distance d+1 and perpendicular-observable interface distance lfloor(d+1)/2rfloor.
items.limits: Numerical/theoretical modeling. Local circuit and resource-state noise rates around 10⁻³ mask interface-distance advantages; benefit requires local noise rates at or below 10⁻⁴.
items.tools: ZX calculus · fusion-based quantum computing (FBQC) · rotated surface codes · fusion boosting
items.abstract: Networking matter-based quantum processing units (QPUs) offers a promising route to scaling fault-tolerant quantum computers. This requires distributed logical operations to be performed across photonic links, where noise is characteristically different from and stronger than in local QPUs owing to photon loss and probabilistic linear-optical operations. Measurement- and fusion-based quantum computing are designed to be robust against loss and probabilistic photonic operations, suggesting they could complement circuit-based error correction at the interface between networked QPUs. We use ZX calculus transformations to construct hybrid syndrome extraction protocols and apply them to distributed rotated surface code lattice surgery, demonstrating that several protocols attain a 50% interface-erasure threshold when local noise is absent, including circuit-based lattice surgery using fused Bell pairs and hybrid protocols using linear cluster states. Relative to a straight Bell-pair interface geometry, the hybrid protocols increase the merge-observable interface distance from d+1 to 2d+1 and restore the perpendicular-observable interface distance from lfloor(d+1)/2rfloor to d. We calculate how the threshold decreases when using truncated resource states and map correctable regions under resource-state errors, local circuit noise, and fusion erasure. We then convert these erasure thresholds into photon-loss thresholds and probe subthreshold performance using fusion boosting. At circuit and resource-state error rates of 10⁻³, local errors largely mask the interface-distance advantage. As local noise is reduced to 10⁻⁴ and below, the linear-chain protocols improve more rapidly with decreasing erasure, suggesting that interface distance enhancements are effective in low local noise regimes.

items.title: Graph Neural Post-selection for Quantum Error Correction
items.authors: Conor Carty, Tamas Noszko, Joschka Roffe, Roberto Bondesan
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: GNN post-selection rejecting 10% of shots reduces per-cycle logical error rates by 3716.6^(+2158.6)_(-1365.4)× for [[72,12,6]] (p=0.001) and 738.2^(+171.1)_(-138.9)× for [[144,12,12]] (p=0.003) bivariate bicycle codes in a single forward pass without extra decoder runs.
items.question: Can graph neural networks accurately predict quantum error correction decoder failure directly from syndromes and single-pass posteriors without running decoders multiple times?
items.prior: For [[72,12,6]] at p=0.001, Q_LLR⁽²⁾ achieved 70.6^(+4.6)_(-4.3)× suppression and 3R-LEC achieved 469.8× at 2.66% rejection.
items.limits: Evaluated on simulated rotated surface and bivariate bicycle quantum memories under uniform depolarising circuit-level noise; requires belief-propagation posteriors for qLDPC codes.
items.tools: Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) · Factor MPNN (FMPNN) · Belief propagation with localized statistics decoding (BP-LSD) · PyMatching (MWPM) · Stim detector error model
items.caption: Per-cycle logical error rate plotted against shot rejection percentage for the [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code at p=0.001, comparing neural post-selection against Q_LLR⁽²⁾ and three-round logical-error criterion baselines.
items.abstract: Post-selection improves the logical reliability of quantum computation by rejecting shots which are likely to result in logical failure. We introduce graph neural networks that predict decoder failure without additional decoder executions, using only syndromes, and for high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, existing belief-propagation posteriors. We evaluate rotated surface and bivariate bicycle (BB) code memories under uniform depolarising circuit-level noise. Retaining 90% of shots gives approximately 3700x and 740x reductions in logical error rates for [[72,12,6]] and [[144,12,12]] BB codes at realistic physical error rates. For the distance 5 surface code at physical noise p=0.003, our neural post-selector achieves logical error suppression comparable to the leading complementary gap method without running the decoder.

items.title: The Robustness of QAC0
items.authors: Daniel Grier, Jackson Morris, Kewen Wu
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Depth-d, size-s QAC circuits on n qubits can be ε-approximated by depth-O(d), size-O(slog²(s/ε)) circuits using only generalized Toffoli, Hadamard, and S gates. Additionally, TC⁰ ⊆EQAC⁰ ∘NC⁰, yielding EQAC⁰ not⊆AC⁰[p] for all primes p.
items.question: Can QAC⁰ circuits be made exact and restricted to a discrete gate set while retaining their computational power beyond AC⁰[p]?
items.prior: Bounded-error QAC⁰ could simulate TC⁰ up to inverse-exponential error using non-standard single-qubit gates outside the Clifford hierarchy (Grier, Morris, Wu 2024).
items.limits: Simulation of TC⁰ requires polynomially many copies of the classical input string; gate compilation is approximate within operator-norm distance ε.
items.tools: exact amplitude amplification · linear combination of unitaries (LCU) · coherent DNF sampling · parallel W-test
items.caption: Conversion schematic showing how an AC⁰[p] circuit C deciding lifted exact Hamming weight EX_(n/2)^(↑n^k) is transformed into circuit tildeC computing unlifted EX_(n/2) by input duplication.
items.abstract: In this work we study the robustness of QAC⁰ with respect to error tolerance and modifications to its gate-set. First, we investigate whether the non-zero error typically allowed for QAC⁰ circuits computing Boolean functions is truly necessary. We show that the error inherent in the parallel W-test of citegrier_morris_wu can be eliminated entirely via a novel application of exact amplitude amplification in the many-copies context. Consequently, we find that QAC⁰ can exactly simulate TC⁰ with polynomially many copies of the classical input and that for every fixed prime p exact QAC⁰, EQAC⁰, can compute total Boolean functions outside of AC⁰[p]. Second, we ask to what extent the computational power of QAC⁰ follows from the fact that arbitrary single-qubit gates may be used at any point in the circuit. We find that QAC⁰ is in fact robust to restrictions on which single-qubit gates are permitted: every QAC⁰ circuit can be approximately implemented by a QAC⁰ circuit consisting of just generalized Toffoli, S, and Hadamard gates. Moreover, this approximating circuit can be constructed efficiently from a classical description of the original circuit.

items.title: Optimal two-mode bosonic loss codes from finite group symmetry
items.authors: Argyris Giannisis Manes, Mahadevan Subramanian, Liang Jiang
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Every best-found two-mode fixed-n bosonic loss code for 4≤n≤25 corresponds to a finite subgroup G⊂SU(2) representation, attaining the linear programming distance bound in 21 of 22 sectors, with binary-polyhedral codes reaching distance d at n_d = lceil(3d²+1)/4rceil through d=10.
items.question: What structure characterizes optimal fixed-total-photon-number two-mode bosonic codes for protecting quantum information against photon loss?
items.prior: Dual-rail encodings and binomial/spin codes (Chuang et al. 1997, Albert et al. 2018, Aydin et al. 2024); prior lowest photon counts for distances d=6,8,10 were larger than (n,d)=(28,6), (49,8), (76,10).
items.limits: Pure photon-loss noise model on two bosonic modes restricted to the fixed-total-excitation subspace; code optimality certified up to n=25, sequence constructions tested through d=10.
items.tools: biconvex alternating semidefinite programming · Knill-Laflamme conditions for finite-group-invariant codes · irreducible spherical tensor decomposition · MacWilliams linear programs with Farkas certificates
items.caption: Phase diagram of loss distance d versus total photon number n. Feasible regions for the SU(2) MacWilliams LP bound are shaded blue, while orange hatched regions are excluded by exact Farkas certificates.
items.abstract: Photon loss is a dominant noise process in bosonic quantum hardware, including superconducting cavities. Fixed-total-photon-number qubit encodings in two bosonic modes retain the loss-detection advantage of dual-rail qubits while supporting photon loss correction. Optimizing entanglement fidelity in this setting for 4≤n≤25 over arbitrary encoders and decoders reveals finite-group structure in every best-found code: 11 correspond to two-dimensional irreducible representations and 11 to reducible ones. Motivated by this emergence, we derive the necessary-and-sufficient Knill-Laflamme conditions for arbitrary finite-group-invariant codes, reducing their construction to equations on representation multiplicity spaces. For every finite subgroup of SU(2) and every tensor rank, we explicitly construct the minimum number of operators required to impose all corresponding loss-correction constraints. These results produce analytic counterparts to most numerical codes and predict constructions missed by the initial search. Exact MacWilliams-Farkas certificates show that our codes achieve the maximum possible loss distance in 21 of the 22 sectors, and we prove that the resulting distance bound is monotone in total photon number. Beyond the scan, we identify a binary-polyhedral sequence with photon number n_d=lceil(3d²+1)/4rceil and construct each corresponding code through distance d=10. To our knowledge, the constructed (n,d)=(28,6),(49,8),(76,10) codes give the smallest reported n for their respective distances; all members through d=9 attain the fixed-n LP distance bound. Together, these constructions, certificates, and a symmetry-reduced constraint count provide evidence for an infinite code family conjectured to attain every distance at the minimum photon number.

items.title: Learned Parallel Bit-Flipping Sequential Belief Propagation Decoding of Quantum LDPC Codes
items.authors: Mohsen Moradi, Taejoon Kim, Remi A. Chou
items.matched: Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes
items.result: Parallel branch exploration using quaternary single-qubit flips achieves the block error rate of T=1000 learned sequential BP at an effective sequential decoding depth of T₀+T_br=200 on the [[288,12,18]] bivariate bicycle code.
items.question: Can parallel bit-flipping branches reduce the decoding latency and escape local traps in reinforcement-learning-scheduled sequential belief propagation for quantum LDPC codes?
items.prior: was RL-S requiring T=1000 iterations to achieve comparable block error rate
items.limits: Depolarizing noise model only; fixed parameters K=25, β=η=0.3, L_BF=25; hardware area scales with branch count K.
items.tools: Quaternary sequential belief propagation · Reinforcement-learning scheduling (Q-table lookahead) · Parallel bit-flipping candidate generation · Depolarizing channel simulation
items.caption: Block error rate versus physical error rate p for the [[288,12,18]] bivariate bicycle code, showing RL-S-BF with depth 200 matches T=1000 RL-S and improves over BP and BPGD by over one order of magnitude at p=0.05.
items.abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes are promising candidates for low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation, but their practical use requires fast, low-complexity, and reliable decoders. Belief propagation (BP) is attractive because of its local message-passing structure, yet standard flooding BP often suffers from convergence failures on QLDPC codes due to short cycles, degeneracy, and symmetric decoding trajectories. Learned sequential BP improves convergence by using a reinforcement-learning policy to choose variable-node update orders, but a single learned trajectory can still be sensitive to unfavorable local Pauli decisions. We propose a learned parallel bit-flipping sequential BP decoder with a new quaternary score combining syndrome gain, a quantized Pauli log-likelihood penalty, and Q-table lookahead at hypothetical post-flip states. Our decoder first runs learned sequential BP for a fixed number of iterations. If the syndrome is not satisfied, it constructs quaternary bit-flipping candidates, each corresponding to changing the current Pauli decision of one qubit. The selected candidates initialize independent learned sequential BP continuations from the same decoder state. Since these continuations are independent, they can be executed in parallel, so testing several candidates mainly increases parallel hardware resources rather than sequential decoding latency. Simulations on representative QLDPC codes over the depolarizing channel show that the proposed decoder improves the reliability of learned sequential BP while having a parallel low-latency structure.

items.title: Sparse Hamiltonian simulation with optimal dependence on the maximum column Euclidean norm
items.authors: Zecheng Li, Chunhao Wang
items.matched: Hamiltonian Simulation by Qubitization
items.result: Simulates d-sparse Hermitian Hamiltonian H with maximum column Euclidean norm normH_(1→2) ≤Λ in O(tΛ√d + √dlog(2/ε)) sparse-oracle queries for tΛ≥1/2. Matches worst-case lower bound when tΛ≥log(2/ε) and d > 1.
items.question: Can the subpolynomial overhead in sparse Hamiltonian simulation scaled by the maximum column Euclidean norm be removed?
items.prior: Was O(τ(log(τ/ε))^(O(√logd))) queries with τ= tΛ√d (Low 2019).
items.limits: Requires tΛ≥1/2 (or tΓ≥1/2 for spectral norm upper bound Γ), d-sparse Hermitian Hamiltonian, and standard sparse-oracle access model.
items.tools: Phase-twisted continuous-time clock · Finite-grid history discretization · Routed private register reuse · Oblivious amplitude amplification (OAA) · Cayley-query quantum walks
items.abstract: We give a quantum algorithm for simulating a d-sparse Hermitian Hamiltonian H, assuming a known upper bound Λ on its maximum column Euclidean norm |H|_(1→2). For tΛ≥1/2, simulation with operator-norm error ε uses \[ O (tΛ√ d+√ dlog(2/ε)) \] sparse-oracle queries. This removes the subpolynomial overhead in Low's algorithm [STOC 2019], replacing it with an additive logarithmic precision term. For d>1 and tΛ≥log(2/ε), the bound matches the worst-case lower bound. A known spectral-norm upper bound may also be used in place of Λ. The number of 1- and 2-qubit gates is linear in the query scale, up to oracle costs and polynomial overhead in the input bit lengths and logarithmic precision parameters. As applications, we obtain O(κ√d polylog(κ/ε)) queries for solving d-sparse quantum linear systems with |A|≤1 and |A⁻¹|≤κ, under standard sparse and state-preparation access. We also give a gate-efficient implementation of black-box unitaries with at most d nonzero entries per row and column using O(√dlog(2/ε)) queries, given sparse access to the unitary and its adjoint. At constant error, the query bound is optimal and yields Θ(√N) queries for arbitrary N×N unitaries, resolving the open question on black-box unitary implementation posed by Berry and Childs [QIC 2012].

items.title: Exponential quantum advantages for decoded quantum interferometry in the streaming setting
items.authors: Kewen Wu, Guangxu Yang
items.matched: quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds
items.result: One-pass quantum streaming solves (α, q, ℓ)-HOPI with O(qℓlogq) space and poly(q,ℓ) time per entry for any approximation α< α_⋆ = (2+√3)/4 ≈93.301%, while any classical p-pass algorithm achieving α> 75% requires space Ωbigl((q^(1+ℓ·κ(α)))/p(ℓlogq)^(-C_αℓ)bigr).
items.question: Does decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) yield unconditional quantum memory advantages in the data streaming setting?
items.limits: Asymptotic in field size q; finite field of prime order q ≥3; trade-off exponent applies for α> 3/4.
items.tools: decoded quantum interferometry · Hermite interpolation · Hasse derivatives · streaming communication lower bounds · Talagrand convex-distance inequality
items.caption: Overview schematic showing how decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) processes input constraints sequentially in a single pass to output a low-degree polynomial satisfying optimal jet constraints.
items.abstract: Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is a polynomial-time quantum algorithm introduced by Jordan et al. (Nature 2025). For a natural optimization problem, known as optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), it achieves approximation guarantees in regimes where all known classical algorithms require exponential time. Besides time, space is another central resource: storing and manipulating a massive input can be very challenging, especially when logical qubits carry substantial fault-tolerant implementation overhead. This motivates the following question: does DQI yield quantum advantages in memory, and can we prove it unconditionally? We give an affirmative answer to this question in the streaming setting. In particular, we consider a natural generalization of OPI using Hermite interpolation and Hasse derivatives, which asks for a low-degree polynomial satisfying as many constraints on its values and derivatives as possible. As a concrete example, we show [Quantum efficiency.] An adaptation of the DQI algorithm produces a polynomial satisfying 93% of the constraints; moreover, it only reads the input stream in one pass, uses polylogarithmic space, and has polylogarithmic computation time per stream entry. [Classical hardness.] Any classical algorithm that produces an answer satisfying just 76% of the constraints requires polynomial space, even if it can read the input stream with polynomially many passes and can use unlimited time. Our result provides a complete tradeoff curve for the tunable parameters, and implies that DQI has provable quantum advantages for the original OPI problem.

items.title: Optimal transducers using symmetries
items.authors: Benoît Dubus, Julien Ladeuze, Jérémie Roland
items.matched: Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…
items.result: Optimal catalyst for quantum state conversion can always be chosen weakly covariant under the problem's symmetry group G, reducing the canonical transducer unitary S^∘ to an intertwiner block-diagonal in the isotypic decomposition. Yields exact optimal transduction complexities W=√(N-M)/(4M) for unstructured search and W=√1-ε²/(2ε) for amplitude amplification.
items.question: How can problem symmetries be exploited to systematically construct optimal quantum transducers and catalysts?

This example shows that a single oracle call is needed with the application of two independent unitaries U₀ and U₁ .
items.abstract: Transducers (Belovs, Jeffery and Yolcu, 2024) are a quantum computing framework describing a quantum algorithm as a unitary converting an input state into a target state using a catalyst, an auxiliary vector that is left unchanged. They are a powerful tool in quantum algorithm design, especially in the context of quantum query complexity: feasible points of the (dual) adversary semidefinite program directly translate into transducers and the optimal transduction complexity is equal to the adversary bound, i.e. the Las Vegas complexity, which is known to characterize bounded-error quantum query complexity. Moreover, contrary to bounded-error algorithms, transducers compose exactly, which limits overheads due to controlling errors in algorithms constructed by composition. Constructing efficient, let alone optimal, transducers in terms of quantum query complexity nevertheless remains a hard task since it still requires solving the adversary SDP and constructing the unitary to obtain an explicit algorithm. In this paper, we show how using the symmetry group of state-conversion problems simplifies both steps. First, using a symmetrization argument, we prove an optimal catalyst can always be chosen covariant under a representation of the symmetry group. Second, we prove that the transducer intertwines two different representations of the group and can thus be chosen block diagonal in the isotypic decomposition of the Hilbert space. Using those methods, we then derive optimal transducers, with optimal constants, for different widely used quantum algorithmic primitives, such as unstructured search, amplitude amplification and amplitude estimation. Our approach extends previous work on the use of representation theory to compute adversary lower bounds (Høyer, Lee, and v Spalek, 2007; Ambainis, Magnin, Roetteler and Roland, 2011) to the systematic construction of optimal algorithms.

items.title: Time-space lower bounds for breaking quantum cryptography
items.authors: Fangqi Dong, Alex Lombardi
items.matched: quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds
items.result: Adversary with S qubits of non-uniform advice making T oracle queries recovers random key k from n-qubit binary phase state |ψ_k⟩ with probability O((T² + √ST)/N) for N=2ⁿ.
items.question: What is the quantitative security of single-copy one-way and pseudorandom states against quantum preprocessing attacks in the quantum random oracle model?
items.prior: Post-quantum one-way functions have inversion probability bound O((T²+ST)/N) (Liu 2023). Post-quantum PRG advantage was O(T/√N + (ST/N)^(1/3)) (Liu 2023), improved here to O(T²/N + √ST/N).
items.limits: Auxiliary-input quantum random oracle model (aux-input QROM). Key space size K ≤N = 2ⁿ.
items.tools: compressed oracles · trace-moment method · operator norm bounding of random matrices
items.abstract: We prove near-optimal time-space lower bounds for breaking quantum cryptography in the random oracle model. Specifically, we show that a T-query adversary with S qubits of non-uniform advice can recover a random key k from the n-qubit binary phase state |ψ_k⟩∝∑_x R(k,x) |x⟩ with probability at most O((T² + √ST)/N) for N=2ⁿ. In contrast, the best known bound for post-quantum one-way functions is O((T² + ST)/N), with a trivial attack at S = N. This demonstrates a new advantage of quantum cryptography over classical cryptography: n qubits of communication suffice for security against preprocessing attacks with space up to N² rather than N. Our methodology is simple: express the optimal preprocessing attack as the operator norm of a random matrix, and bound this value in expectation over the random oracle via the trace-moment method. These trace moments have a natural interpretation using compressed oracles [Zhandry, Crypto 2019], which we then analyze. This can be viewed as a simplification and generalization of the approach of Liu [Eurocrypt 2023] for proving time-space tradeoffs for breaking post-quantum cryptography. We also prove the following results: (1) We tighten Liu's analysis of post-quantum PRGs in QROM, achieving a distinguishing advantage bound of O(fracT²N + √fracSTN). (2) For unitary synthesis, we extend the one-query lower bound of Lombardi-Ma-Wright [STOC 2024] to hold against adversaries that can make one arbitrary function query along with polynomially many (adaptive) queries to the random oracle, either before or after the function query. This also interprets the original LMW24 result in terms of compressed oracles. (3) Finally, we prove a tight O(frac√SN) bound for the pseudorandomness of random binary phase states against space S distinguishers.
